wiki_excerpt:
Ryūnosuke Akutagawa (芥川 龍之介, Akutagawa Ryūnosuke; Japanese pronunciation: [ɾʲɯː.no.sɯ̥.ke], 1 March 1892 – 24 July 1927), art name Chōkōdō Shujin (澄江堂主人), was a Japanese writer active in the Taishō period in Japan. He is regarded as the "father of the Japanese short story", and Japan's premier literary award, the Akutagawa Prize, is named after him. He took his own life at the age of 35 through an overdose of barbital.


Early life
Ryūnosuke Akutagawa was born in Irifune, Kyōbashi, Tokyo City (present-day Akashi, Chūō, Tokyo), the eldest son of businessman Toshizō Niihara and his wife, Fuku. His father served in the Boshin War, and later founded a successful dairy business. His mother experienced mental illness shortly after his birth, so he was adopted and raised by the family of his maternal uncle, Michiaki Akutagawa, from whom he received the Akutagawa family name. The Akutagawa lineage was part of the warrior class and served the Tokugawa clan as okubōzu, who managed the tearoom and served tea. The Akutagawas looked down upon Ryūnosuke's father as a "parvenu". Ryūnosuke's adoptive family enjoyed art. He was interested in classical Chinese literature from an early age, as well as in the works of Mori Ōgai and Natsume Sōseki.
He entered the First Higher School in 1910, without taking entrance exams thanks to his middle school academic record, and developed relationships with classmates such as Kan Kikuchi, Masao Kume, Yūzō Yamamoto, and Tsuchiya Bunmei, all of whom would later become authors. He began writing after entering Tokyo Imperial University (now the University of Tokyo) in 1913, where he studied English literature. While still a student, he proposed marriage to a childhood friend, Yayoi Yoshida, but his adoptive family did not approve of the union. In 1916 he became engaged to Fumi Tsukamoto, whom he married in 1918. They had three children: Hiroshi Akutagawa (1920–1981) was an actor, Takashi Akutagawa (1922–1945) was killed as a student draftee in Burma, and Yasushi Akutagawa (1925–1989) was a composer.
Following graduation, Akutagawa taught briefly at the Naval Engineering School in Yokosuka, Kanagawa as an English language instructor, before deciding to devote his efforts to writing fulltime.


Literary career

In 1914, Akutagawa and his former high school friends revived the literary journal Shinshichō ("New Currents of Thought"), where they published translations of William Butler Yeats and Anatole France along with works they had written themselves. Akutagawa published his second short story Rashōmon the following year in the literary magazine Teikoku Bungaku ("Imperial Literature"), while still a student. The story, based on a twelfth-century tale, was not well received by Akutagawa's friends, who greatly criticized it. Nonetheless, Akutagawa gathered up the courage to visit his idol, Natsume Sōseki, in December 1915 for Sōseki's weekly literary circles. In November, he published the work in the literary magazine Teikoku Mongaku. In early 1916 he published Hana ("The Nose", 1916), which received a letter of praise from Sōseki and secured Akutagawa his first taste of fame.
It was also at this time that Akutagawa started writing haiku under the haigo (pen name) Gaki (我鬼). Akutagawa followed with a series of short stories set in Heian period, Edo period or early Meiji period Japan. These stories reinterpreted classical works and historical incidents often revolving around the Konjaku Monogatarishū. Examples of these stories include: Gesaku zanmai ("Absorbed in Letters", 1917) and Kareno-shō ("Gleanings from a Withered Field", 1918), Jigokuhen ("Hell Screen", 1918); Hōkyōnin no Shi ("The Death of a Disciple", 1918), and Butōkai ("The Ball", 1920). Akutagawa was a strong opponent of naturalism. He published Mikan ("Mandarin Oranges", 1919) and Aki ("Autumn", 1920) which have more modern settings.

Born in Tokyo on March 1, 1892, he produced over 150 short stories during his brief career, drawing from traditional Japanese and Chinese sources as well as European influences to explore themes of psychology, the supernatural, and human frailty. His most famous works, including "RashÅmon" (1915) and "In a Bamboo Grove" (1922), were later adapted by director Akira Kurosawa into the 1950 film RashÅmon, which earned international acclaim, including the Grand Prix at the Venice Film Festival. Akutagawa's life ended tragically by suicide on July 24, 1927, at age 35, leaving a legacy honored by Japan's prestigious Akutagawa Prize for emerging writers, established in 1935. Akutagawa was born into a middle-class family in Tokyo 's KyÅbashi district as the only son (third child) of Niihara ToshizÅ, a dairy operator, and Niihara Fuku. Following his mother's onset of mental illness shortly after his birth, he was adopted and raised primarily by his maternal uncle and a nanny, from whom he took the Akutagawa surname. His mother passed away when he was ten; Akutagawa himself later experienced hallucinations and health issues. He excelled academically, studying English literature at Tokyo Imperial University from 1913, where he was mentored by the renowned novelist Natsume SÅseki, who encouraged his early literary efforts. After graduating in 1916, Akutagawa briefly taught English at a naval engineering school and worked as a reporter and editor for the Osaka Mainichi newspaper starting in 1921, while dedicating himself to writing. His literary style blended modernist techniques with romantic and grotesque elements, often featuring unreliable narrators, moral ambiguity, and supernatural motifs reminiscent of Edgar Allan Poe, whose works Akutagawa translated. Key stories like "The Spider's Thread" (1918), a Buddhist parable of redemption, and "The Hell Screen" (1918), a tale of artistic obsession and torment, showcase his innovative adaptations of classical tales into psychological narratives. Later works, such as the satirical novella Kappa (1927), critiqued modern society through fantastical lenses, reflecting his growing disillusionment with Japan's rapid Westernization during the TaishÅ era (1912â1926). Akutagawa's influence extends globally, with his stories translated into numerous languages and inspiring adaptations beyond Kurosawa's film, cementing his status as one of Japan's most important early 20th-century authors. Despite his short life, marked by overwork, insomnia, and mental strain, his precise prose and exploration of human darkness continue to resonate in world literature. The Akutagawa Prize, awarded annually since 1935 by the Society for the Promotion of Japanese Literature, underscores his enduring impact on contemporary Japanese fiction.
